data.title: Tollense – the oldest known battle of the Bronze Age
data.excerpt: Around 1250 BC thousands of warriors clashed on the river Tollense in northern Germany, and the bones of at least 130 men are changing the way we think about warfare in the Bronze Age. This report from the journal Science was translated and put together for us by our collaborator Martin Schuster – travel back more than 3,000 years with it.

children.text: We bring you a very topical article about a new discovery – the remains of a terrible Bronze Age war in Germany. Great thanks for the translation and for putting the article together go to our collaborator Martin Schuster. Travel back more than 3,000 years, to the time when a savage Bronze Age battle was fought.

The March issue of the prestigious and respected journal Science carried a study of a large and brutal battle on the river Tollense, which brings new insights into the manner of fighting and the organisation of life in the Bronze Age.

An excavation at an ancient battlefield in northern Germany has revealed signs of a great battle, indicated for example by the density of the bones, as can be seen in this photograph from 2013. …1,478 bones were found, including 20 skulls.

About 3,200 years ago, two armies met while attempting to cross a river near the Baltic Sea. This confrontation cannot be …from history textbooks – the written word did not become common in this area for another 2,000 years. But this was no skirmish between local clans. Thousands of warriors met in brutal combat, perhaps even in a single day, using weapons made of wood, flint and bronze, the metal that in that age defined the very best quality of military technology.

The warriors tried to find firm ground underfoot on the bank of the river Tollense, a narrow strip of water that flows through the marshes of northern Germany towards the Baltic Sea. The armies fought man against man, maiming and killing one another with war clubs, spears, swords and knives. Arrows with bronze and flint heads were shot at close range, punching through skulls and lodging deep in the bones of young men. Horses belonging to high-ranking warriors collapsed into the mud after being fatally impaled. Not everyone stood face to face with the enemy: some warriors broke, fled the fight and were cut down from behind.

When the fighting was over, hundreds of bodies lay dead, scattered across the marshy valley. Some bodies were stripped of their valuables and bobbed in the shallow water; others sank to the bottom, and the depth protected them from looting. Peat deposits covered the bones over time, and as the centuries passed, the bloody battle was forgotten.

In 1996 an amateur archaeologist found a piece of bone from an upper arm, the bone sticking out of the steep river bank. This was the first clue that the Tollense Valley, about 120 kilometres north of Berlin, was hiding a terrible secret. The flint of an arrowhead was firmly embedded in one end of the humerus, and it prompted archaeologists to dig a small test trench, which yielded more bones, a shattered skull and a 73-centimetre club resembling a baseball bat. All the artefacts were radiocarbon dated to around 1250 BC, which suggests that they come from a single episode of the European Bronze Age.

children.text: Now, after a series of excavations between 2009 and 2015, researchers have begun to understand the battle and its surprising implications for Bronze Age society. Along a three-kilometre stretch of the river Tollense, archaeologists from the Mecklenburg-Vorpommern Department of Historic Preservation (MVPDHP) and from the University of Greifswald (UG) have discovered wooden clubs, bronze spearheads and arrowheads of flint and bronze. They also found an enormous quantity of bones: the remains of at least five horses and more than 100 men. The bones of hundreds more that may remain unrecovered, and the thousands more who may have fought but survived, suggest the enormous scale of the battle.

“If our hypothesis is correct, that all the finds belong to the same event, then we are dealing with a conflict on a scale so far completely unknown north of the Alps,” says the co-director of the excavations Thomas Terberger, an archaeologist at the Lower Saxony State Office for Cultural Heritage in Hanover. “We know of nothing comparable.” It can even be compared – weapons and warriors included – with a battle of this size anywhere in antiquity.

Northern Europe in the Bronze Age was long underrated as a backwater, overshadowed by the more sophisticated civilisations of the Near East and Greece. Bronze itself was created in the Near East around 3200 BC and it took 1,000 years to reach here. But the scale at Tollense points to greater organisation – and more violence – than has been thought until now. “Up to now the scenarios considered were raids by small groups of young men, killing and stealing food, but to imagine such a large fight with thousands of people is very surprising,” says Svend Hansen, head of the Eurasia Department of the German Archaeological Institute (DAI) in Berlin. The well-preserved bones and artefacts have added detail to this picture of a more advanced Bronze Age, pointing to the existence of a trained warrior class and suggesting that people from all over Europe entered the bloody fight.

Tollense is something special. “As far as the Bronze Age is concerned, we lacked evidence; now we have a battlefield, dead people and weapons, all together,” says University College Dublin (UCD) archaeologist Barry Molloy. “We have obtained the evidence.”

A lakeside hunting lodge named Schloss Wiligrad was built at the turn of the 19th century, deep in the forest, 14 kilometres north of Schwerin, the capital of the northern German federal state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Today the building houses both departments of the state institution for the preservation of historic monuments and a small local art museum.

In a high-ceilinged room on the second floor of the castle, tall windows look out over the mist-shrouded lake. Inside, pale winter light illuminates dozens of skulls arranged on shelves and tables. In the middle of the room, the long bones of the lower limbs and short ribs lie in tight rows on a table; further remains are stored in paper boxes stacked on metal shelving that reaches almost to the ceiling. The bones take up so much space that there is barely room to walk through.

When the first of these finds was dug out in 1996, it was not yet clear that Tollense had been a battlefield. Some archaeologists thought the bones might be from a flooded cemetery, or that they had been washed in over the centuries.

There was reason for scepticism. Before Tollense there was little direct evidence of large-scale violence in the Bronze Age, particularly in this region. Historical accounts from the Near East and Greece described epic battles, but few artefacts confirmed those grand reports. “Even in Egypt, despite hearing many stories about wars, we have never found such substantial archaeological evidence of their participants and their victims,” says Molloy of UCD.

In Bronze Age Europe …historical accounts of any war, and all the researchers explained the weapons in graves as ceremonial burial, and a few mass graves with unquestionable evidence of violence, such as executed bodies or arrowheads embedded in bones. Before 1990, “for a long time we had no reason for any real belief in warfare in the distant past,” says Hansen of the DAI. Grave goods were explained rather as prestige objects or symbols of power than as real weapons. “Most people thought that ancient civilisations were peaceful and that the Bronze Age was about trade and the like,” says Helle Vangkilde, an archaeologist at Aarhus University in Denmark. “Very little was said about waging war.”
Fig. 4 Archaeologists have discovered a vast quantity of artefacts from the battlefield.

The 10,000 bones in this room – what is left of the defeated of Tollense – changed everything. They were found densely packed in underground caches: in one such place, 1,478 bones, among them 20 skulls, were found crammed into a space of only 12 square metres. Archaeologists think that the bodies ended up, or were piled, in shallow pools, where the movement of the water mixed the bones of different individuals. By counting individual bones – skulls and femurs, for example – UG forensic anthropologists Ute Brinker and Annemarie Schramm identified at least 130 individuals, almost exclusively men, mostly aged between 20 and 30.

The number of bones suggests the scale of the battle. “We have at least 130 people and five horses. And we have opened only 450 square metres. That is at most 10% of the find layer, and perhaps only 3% or 4%,” says Detlef Jantzen, chief archaeologist at the MVDHP. “If we uncovered the whole area, we could have 750 people. That is an incredible number for the Bronze Age.” As they admit in their restrained estimates, both he and Terberger argue that if one in five participants was killed in the battle and left on the battlefield, it could mean that almost 4,000 warriors took part in the fighting.

Brinker, the forensic anthropologist in charge of analysing the remains, says that the moisture and chemical composition of the soil in the Tollense valley preserved the bones almost perfectly. “We can reconstruct exactly what happened,” she says, pointing to a rib with two small V-shaped cuts on one edge. “These cut marks on the rib mean that he was stabbed twice in the same place. We have many of them, often several marks on the same rib.”
Fig. 5 A bronze arrow penetrated the skull and reached the brain

Scanning of the bones using micro-computed tomography at a materials science institute in Berlin and at the University of Rostock has produced detailed 3D images of these injuries. Archaeologists are now identifying the weapons responsible by comparing the images with scans of weapons found at Tollense or in contemporary graves elsewhere in Europe. Diamond-shaped holes in bones, for example, match the shape of the bronze arrowheads found on the battlefield strikingly well. (Bronze artefacts occur more frequently than flint ones at Tollense, perhaps because metal detectors were used to search through the spoil heaps in order to recover artefacts).

The bone scans have also produced a more precise picture of how the battle unfolded, says Terberger. According to an X-ray of the humerus with the arrowhead – the one that triggered the discovery of the battlefield – it appeared to show signs of healing. In a 2011 paper in Antiquity, the group suggested the idea that the man had suffered the injury earlier in the battle but had been able to fight for several days or weeks before his death, which could mean that the conflict was not a single clash but a series of skirmishes lasting several weeks.

Microscopic examination of this wound told a different story: what at first looked like healing – an opaque mass around the arrowhead on the X-ray – was in fact a layer of shattered bone, compressed by a single impact that was probably fatal. “That forces us to revise the idea that this happened over the course of several weeks,” says Terberger. So far no bodies show healed wounds, so it is likely that the battle took place on just one day, or at most over a few days. “If we are dealing with a single event, which is more likely than skirmishes over several weeks, that has a great impact on our interpretation of the scale of the conflict.”

In the past year, a team of engineers in Hamburg used technology developed for modelling collisions of aircraft components in order to understand what kinds of wounds the fighters suffered. For example, archaeologists at first thought that the warrior whose femur cracked near the hip joint must have fallen from a horse. The injury resembles those that result today from a motorcycle crash or a riding accident.

But the modelling told a different story. Melanie Schwinning and Hella Harten-Buga, archaeologists and engineers at the University of Hamburg, took into account the physical properties of bone and of bronze weapons, together with examples of injuries from a fall from a horse. Using experimental archaeology, they repeatedly drove flint and bronze points into dead pigs and recorded the damage.

Schwinning and Harten-Buga said that they drove a bronze spearhead into the bone at a sharp downward angle in order to be able to break the thigh, and it cracked in half like a log. “When we modelled it, it looks much more like a hand weapon than a fall from a horse,” says Schwinning. “We could even have increased the force, but it was not necessary.” They estimate that an average-sized man with his body weight drives a spear in with sufficient force.

Why men gathered at this place to fight and die is another mystery that the archaeological evidence is helping to unravel. The Tollense Valley is narrow here, in some places only 50 metres wide. It is partly boggy, while elsewhere it offers firm ground underfoot. The place may have been a kind of choke point for travellers moving across the north European plain.

In 2013, geomagnetic surveys revealed evidence of a 120-metre-long bridge or causeway stretching across the valley. During two seasons of excavation, the buried structures proved to be made of wooden posts and stone. Radiocarbon dating showed that although much of the structure predated the battle by more than 500 years, some of its parts may have been built or renewed at the time of the battle, which suggests that the causeway could have been in continuous use for centuries – and also a widely known landmark in the landscape.

“The crossing played an important role in the conflict. Perhaps one group tried to cross it and the other pushed it back,” says Terberger. “The conflict began there and the fighting spread along the river.”
Fig. 6 The peaceful meanders of the river Tollense today, once the scene of savage fighting.

The victors could then take from the bodies whatever valuables they could carry and then threw the corpses into shallow water, which protected them from carnivores and birds. The bones are ungnawed and other marks typical of the action of scavengers are also absent.

Elsewhere the team found people and horses that had remained buried a metre or two deeper, at a place where the river bed ran in the Bronze Age. Mixed in with these remains were gold rings, probably hair rings, spiral rings of tin perhaps worn by a man on his fingers, and tiny bronze spirals that probably served as decoration. These dead must have fallen, or been thrown, into the deeper parts of the river and sank quickly to the bottom, where their valuables escaped the clutches of robbers.

At the time of the battle, northern Europe appears to have been without towns or even small villages. According to archaeologists, it can be said that the people here were loosely connected by culture to Scandinavia and lived with their extended families on individual farmsteads, with a population density of less than five people per square kilometre. The nearest known large settlement of this period is more than 350 kilometres to the south-east, at Watenstedt. It was a landscape not unlike the farming parts of Europe today, but without roads, telephones or radio.

And yet chemical traces in the remains suggest that most of the warriors of Tollense came from hundreds of kilometres away. The isotopes in your teeth correspond to the food and water you consumed during childhood, which in turn reflects the surrounding geology of the place where you grew up. Doug Price, a retired archaeologist of the University of Wisconsin, Madison, analysed strontium, oxygen and carbon isotopes in 20 teeth from Tollense. Only a few showed values typical of the north European plains, which extend from the Netherlands to Poland. The other teeth came from further away, although Price cannot yet say exactly where from. “The range of isotope values is really large,” he says. “We can, however, conclude that the dead came from many different places.”

Further clues come from the isotope of another element, nitrogen, which reflects diet. The nitrogen isotopes in the teeth of some of the men suggest that they ate a diet rich in millet, which at that time was more common in southern than in northern Europe.

Ancient DNA could potentially reveal much more: compared with other Bronze Age samples from across Europe in this period, it could point to the homeland of the warriors, as well as such details as eye and hair colour. Genetic analysis is only in its beginnings, but so far it supports the idea of distant origins. DNA from the teeth suggests that some of the warriors are connected with modern southern Europeans and others with people living in present-day Poland and in Scandinavia. “This is not a bunch of local idiots,” says University of Mainz geneticist Joachim Burger. “It is a very diverse population.”

As Vangkilde of the University of Aarhus says: “It is an army like the one described in Homer’s epics, made up of smaller war bands that were gathered together to sack Troy” – which was supposed to have happened almost 100 years later, in 1184 BC. “That could mean an unexpectedly broad social organisation,” says Jantzen. “If you want to arrange a battle over such an enormous distance and gather all these people in one place, that is a tremendous achievement,” he says.

So far the team has published only a handful of peer-reviewed papers. They have halted the excavations, are waiting for a larger volume of funding and are now writing a publication. But archaeologists familiar with the project say that the implications are dramatic. Tollense may force a reassessment of the whole period in the area from the Baltic to the Mediterranean, says archaeologist Kristian Kristiansen of the University of Gothenburg in Sweden. “It opens the door to a great deal of new evidence about the way Bronze Age societies were organised,” he says.

For example, strong evidence suggests that this was not the first battle for these men. Twenty-seven per cent of the skeletons showed the first signs of healed wounds from earlier fighting, including three skulls with healed fractures. “It is hard to say the reason for their injuries, but they do not look like typical injuries of young farmers,” says Jantzen.
Fig. 7
This skull discovered in the Tollense valley shows clear evidence of blunt-force trauma, perhaps from a club.

The standardised metal weapons and the remains of horses that were found mixed with human bones at one spot suggest that at least some of the warriors were well equipped and well trained. “These were not farmer-soldiers who went out every few years for some brawl,” says Terberger. “These are professional fighters.”

Body armour and shields appeared in northern Europe in the centuries just before the beginning of the conflict at Tollense, and their emergence may have been forced by the needs of militarised societies. “If you have to fight with body armour, helmets and cuirasses, either you need daily training, or you cannot move,” says Hansen. That is the reason why, for example, the biblical David, a shepherd, refused armour and a bronze helmet before fighting Goliath. “This kind of training is essential for special groups of warriors,” says Hansen. At Tollense, these bronze-clad mounted warriors could have been a kind of officer class, commanding grumbling foot soldiers carrying simpler weapons.

But why did so much military force converge in a narrow river valley in northern Germany? Kristiansen says that this period appears to have been an era of significant upheaval from the Mediterranean to the Baltic. In Greece, at about the time of the battle at Tollense, the sophisticated Mycenaean civilisation collapsed; in Egypt the pharaohs boasted of defeating the “Sea Peoples”, raiders from distant lands who overthrew the neighbouring Hittites. And shortly after Tollense, the scattered farmsteads of northern Europe began to concentrate into fortified settlements of the kind known from the southern regions. “Around 1200 BC there is a radical change in the direction of society and culture,” says Vangkilde. “Tollense fits into a period when the fires of war spread everywhere.”

Tollense looks like the first step towards a way of life that we know even today. From the scale and brutality of the battle to the presence of a military elite wielding sophisticated weapons, the events of that distant day are connected with more familiar and more recent conflicts. “It could be the first evidence of a break in social organisation and in fighting in Europe,” says Vangkilde.

Translator’s notes:

So much for the massacre on the river Tollense from the magazine Science and the author of the article. But it would not be the academic community if a debate had not been stirred up, with attempts to interpret the battle in a somewhat different way and, knowing how things go, also with an effort to draw attention to oneself. Out of the scholarly diversity of opinions and non-binding disputation the most probable result will in the end emerge.

In my view a very well-informed man, who blogs on this subject under the nickname Serbian Irish, came up with the idea that this was not a clash of two armies but an enormous armed raid on a large caravan. Among other things, he argues that skeletons of women and children were also found among the remains, which could indeed have been women warriors and porters, but could equally have been travellers in a caravan. A further argument is the gold, brass and tin ingots that were found, which he considers more likely to have been trade goods than ornaments of warriors. From time immemorial travelling merchants banded together into the largest possible caravans, an inseparable part of which were well-armed and well-trained warriors, and he assumes that the caravan was carrying trade goods from the area of the Ore Mountains and Silesia, regions of the Bronze Age Únětice culture known for their mineral wealth and its processing, in today’s Krušné hory and Krkonoše mountains, and that the hired protection came from still further south, even from Mediterranean regions.
You can find out much more, with maps and photographic documentation, at the link:
http://oldeuropeanculture.blogspot.sk/2015/07/tollense-battle.html

The Poles, for their part, assume that the inhabitants of present-day Poland at that time joined forces with the powers of antiquity and pushed the predecessors of the Vikings back to the north, thereby preventing their exodus in the face of climate change in the north and their subjugation of Central Europe.
